The male and female faculties have the sense of predominance with respect to the ability to continue the lineage through descendants.

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), as a single category, possesses a predominant influence over the various activities, applications, and efforts of one who lives by means of the causes and conditions for sustaining life;
among these, pleasure (*sukha*) is foremost.
Equanimity is the last.
Thus, these five faculties have a predominant influence over the enjoyment of the desirable fruits produced by past karma and the creation of new karma;
faith is the first among them.
Wisdom follows as their culmination.
Thus, these five faculties have the sense of being predominant for progressing toward detachment from worldly desires.

The three untainted faculties—*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*, *ājñendriya*, and *ājñātāvīndriya*—have the sense of being predominant for attaining the ultimate goal of progressing toward supramundane detachment.
Whatever meanings are perceived by all the world, they are exhausted in this measure alone.
One should know that as for those meanings that can lead to ultimate realization,
there is nothing that transcends these twenty-two faculties.
All faculties are subsumed within twenty-two;
therefore, the verse says:
"The faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body."
Male and female, as well as life and intention;
suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity;
faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
That which has not yet arisen and that which has already ceased are fully known;
these are called the twenty-two [faculties].

The first five material faculties have as their nature the pure matter (rūpa-prasāda) of the eye and so forth, which are transformations produced by the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) and other [consciousnesses].
The male and female faculties are subsumed under the body faculty;
therefore, they take a small portion thereof as their nature.

The life-faculty (jīvitendriya), however, is merely a provisional designation based on a particular state of the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) and does not possess a separate intrinsic nature.
The faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) has, in general, volitional formations and consciousness as its nature.
The five faculties of feeling each have their respective feelings as their nature.
The five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) have faith, energy (*vīrya*), and pure mindfulness (*smṛti*) and so forth as their respective intrinsic natures.

Regarding the faculty of "knowing the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), it is held that within the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*), the application (*prayoga*), and the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the five faculties—faith and the others—as well as the mental faculty, joy, pleasure, and equanimity, constitute the nature of this faculty during their subsequent moments within these three states.
All the nine untainted faculties, beginning with faith, that exist from the final moment of the path of seeing through the path of cultivation up to the diamond-like concentration,
are all of the nature of the faculty of "having known" (ājñātāvīndriya).

The nine untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) of all those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) are entirely of the nature of the faculty of one who has perfect knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
That "seed" is merely another name for "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*).
However, there are generally three kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The first is the habitual tendency of names and expressions (*nāma-vyañjana-vāsanā*).
There are two types of names and expressions.
First is the designation that expresses meaning,
which refers to the specific vocal sounds capable of signifying an object;
only the sixth consciousness can take this name as its cognitive object.
However, names are merely specific variations of vocal sounds and are exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta) in nature;
they cannot permeate (vāsanā) to form seeds for matter (rūpa), mind (citta), and so forth.

However, because of names, the mind undergoes transformation in accordance with those names, appearing as the five aggregates, the phenomena of the three natures, and so forth, thereby forming perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Because names give rise to seeds, these are called "seeds of verbal expression" (*nāma-kalpa-bīja*).
All perfuming and seeds are brought about by mental factors (*caitta*).
The seeds perfumed by the mind, through internal causes and external conditions,
manifest as the two types of objective representation and linguistic expression;
these are precisely the minds and mental factors that are capable of cognizing objects.
This refers to all the mind-streams consisting of the seeing-aspects (*darśana-bhāga*) of the seven consciousnesses;
it does not refer to the aspect-aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*),
which cannot manifest objects.
It is the engagement with various types of objects of perception according to their meanings,
based on conventional designations,
and the conceptual differentiation of various types of objects of perception according to their meanings.
The habitual tendencies of the two types of self-grasping are also of two kinds:
first, the innate;
second, the conceptually constructed.
This refers to the seeds of false attachment to "self" and "what belongs to self," which,
following the perfuming of the two types of self-attachment,
form seeds that cause the distinction between self and other among sentient beings and so forth.
Third is the habitual tendency of the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*),
which refers to the seeds of karma that bring about maturation (*vipāka*) within the three realms.
This, too, is of two kinds.
First, contaminated wholesome [karma],
which is karma that can bring about desirable results;
second, all unwholesome [karma].
This refers to karma that brings about undesirable results.
This point is set forth in the eighth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
The phrase "this excludes the resultant mind and mental factors" means:
Among the four types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*),
the latter three are capable of perfuming because they are powerful;
only the very first, the maturation-neutral (*vipāka-avyākṛta*), is not.
If the eighth consciousness cannot be perfumed at all,
and if among the six consciousnesses there are those of an indeterminate nature,
these are of two kinds.
The Victorious One (the Buddha) possesses attachment to the Dharma and is thus capable of perfuming;
those who are inferior lack such attachment and are therefore incapable of perfuming.
The term "equal" used here includes this distinction.
If that is so, from what does this nature-seed arise?
Since it would then be without a seed, from what could it manifest?
Answer:
Because seeds are of two kinds:
first, those that are innate;
second, those that are newly perfumed.
Although these types of indeterminate states are not newly perfumed,
they arise from seeds existing by nature; therefore,
even though they are not produced through perfuming, there is no fault.
If that is so, the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) should also be like this.
Why, then, must the first seven [consciousnesses] perfuse seeds?
Answer:
In reality, both types must necessarily arise together;
if one were to speak of only one, it would constitute a logical error.
Therefore, even inferior neutral states are established as being perfumed by and arising from all six consciousnesses.
This point is somewhat difficult;
it should be further examined with careful scrutiny.
Therefore, regarding the statement that the Tathāgata’s eighth pure consciousness (viśuddha-vijñāna) carries only the seeds of the past and so forth:
Since it has already been refuted that the wholesome and the defiled are not what is perfumed,
and since the Buddha’s eighth consciousness is exclusively wholesome and therefore not what is perfumed,
there arises this objection:
If it were neither that which is perfumed nor that which perfumes,
then the state of Buddhahood would have no seeds;
how then could it give rise to all the dharmas of merit?
To resolve this objection, it is said:
"Pure consciousness carries only pre-existing seeds and does not undergo new perfuming;
when it is said that the seeds of its image and perception are perfumed, [it refers to those pre-existing seeds]."
As stated in the eighth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*:
"The first seven consciousnesses can infuse seeds of both the aspect (nimitta) and the seeing (darśana) into the eighth [consciousness].
This is explained according to the doctrine of "newly infused" (*navya-abhyāsa*) held by Nanda.
If one explains according to the view of Ratnamati regarding the theory of "original existence" (mūlataḥ sattva),
the perfuming by the first seven consciousnesses merely causes [the seeds] to increase,
because the objective basis (ālambana) upon which they rely is neutral (avyākṛta).
The essence [of these] is that within the eighth consciousness, the nature of both the image-part (nimittabhāga) and the seeing-part (darśanabhāga) is indeterminate (avyākṛta).
As for the image-parts that arise which are neither wholesome nor unwholesome,
these are the image-parts that are reflections of the seven evolving consciousnesses.
If the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) transformed by the first six consciousnesses were produced from substantial entities,
it would be a "real object" (svabhāva-viṣaya) and thus would not conform to its subjective aspect (darśana-bhāga);
consequently, it would not be [morally] wholesome or unwholesome.
If the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) perfumed by the seventh consciousness is a "concrete" object (sadravyālambana)—
even though it encompasses both the phenomenal and the fundamental [aspects], and is exclusively non-defined (avyākṛta) due to being either obscured (nivṛta) or unobscured (anivṛta)—
it nevertheless takes defiled and pure phenomena as its objects and evolves in dependence upon them.
This means that the first six consciousnesses take defiled and pure objects as their conditions, giving rise to defiled and pure appearances and thereby undergoing transformation through appearance.
Although they may practice generosity and other virtues, they cannot eliminate these appearances;
this is entirely because the defiled manas serves as the support for these consciousnesses.
While that [manas] has not yet been extinguished, it functions by discerning signs;
once the manas has been extinguished, its functioning regarding signs is liberated.
Therefore, the first six consciousnesses take defiled and pure phenomena as their objects.
All are established based upon the manas.
Although there is matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*), there is no matter that is the fruit of karma (*karma-phala-rūpa*).
This refers to the various objective appearances of matter and so forth manifested by noble ones (*ārya*) and those with mastery over meditative concentration.
That which has meditative concentration as its cause is called "matter that is the fruit of concentration.
If the bodily forms and other characteristics produced by the karmic causes of ordinary beings and noble ones are present, they are called "matter that is the fruit of karma.
Those who have not yet attained meditative concentration possess only matter that is the fruit of karma.
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is only the fruit of meditative concentration.
If one is among those such as Arhats on the supramundane path (lokottaramārga) in the heavens of the form realm (rūpadhātu), both types of matter (rūpa) are absent.
Because the afflicted mind (kliṣṭamanas) has operated subtly, as a single homogeneous class, spontaneously since beginningless time,
it cannot be suppressed or extinguished by any mundane path with outflows (sāsrava-mārga). However,
there is the sense that it can be suppressed and extinguished by the noble paths of the three vehicles (triyāna-āryamārga).
Because the understanding of true selflessness contradicts the grasping at a self,
when the subsequently attained uncontaminated state manifests,
it is its outflow and likewise contradicts this [grasping].
Because both the realization of true non-self and its subsequently attained cognition are untainted (*anāsrava*),
they are called the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*). Since the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is an outflow (*nisyanda*) of the noble path, it is likewise so designated.
Because it is utterly quiescent,
this too does not exist;
yet, because its seeds have not been permanently severed, it is not non-existent.
Having emerged from the noble path after the meditative attainment of cessation,
these [wholesome factors] manifest once again and continue to do so until they are extinguished;
thus, the reflections of all wholesome dharmas are constantly present before one.
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"For example, it is like a bright mirror placed upon a high tower;
if the objects of the world are not situated at a great distance, in darkness, or behind obstructions,"
All appear as reflected images within the mirror.

In this same way, the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom abides upon the principle of the *dharmadhātu-tathatā* (the suchness of the realm of phenomena) for all sentient beings who are neither ignorant nor deluded and are free from obstructions.
The reflections of all wholesome dharmas appear therein;
that is to say, those which coexist with all natures, stages, and times.
Regarding "all natures":
This refers to the wholesome, the unwholesome, the obscured-unspecified,
and the unobscured-unspecified.
"All stages" refers specifically to the nine stages.
The four dhyānas of the desire realm and the four formless attainments constitute nine.
Regarding "at all times":
whenever the eight consciousnesses arise, there is no time when they do not exist.
"Coexistent with all" means that it always arises in association with all minds and mental factors.
"The wholesome exists as a single [type] and is present in all stages" means:
However, there are two kinds of "all stages" (sarvabhūmi).
If one refers to the first nine stages as "all stages," then pliancy (praśrabdhi) does not belong to all stages,
as it is absent from the desire realm.
If those states possessing vitarka and so forth are called "all stages," then pliancy (praśrabdhi) indeed extends to the first dhyāna as well,
because pliancy exists in the stage characterized by vitarka and vicāra.
Regarding "all four are non-defiled":
this means that both root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are collectively termed "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*).
Because they do not extend to the wholesome, they do not comprise all natures.
They do not pervade the three realms nor all stages;
they are absent during moments of wholesome mind and are not present at all times;
they do not arise simultaneously with the head [of the thought] nor are they all co-existent.
Since greed, delusion, pride, and so forth also pervade all three realms,
how can it be said that they do not exist in all stages?
Answer:
Although craving, ignorance, and so forth pertain to all nine stages,
the affliction of anger exists only in the desire realm;
because it is not present in all [stages], it does not belong to all stages.
Since the secondary afflictions (upakleśa) lack all four of these characteristics that apply to the root afflictions (mūlakleśa),
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* combines them into one category.
Taken together, there are five stages.
Regarding the statement, "this [mental factor] should awaken the seeds of the mind that are to arise," it means that the nature of this *manasikāra* (attention) is capable of awakening them.
If these seeds startle and cause other seeds of mind and mental factors to arise as actualities,
and if they reach the stage of actuality and lead them toward their respective objects,
then although these [seeds] arise simultaneously with the mind, [they function as its causes].
However, there is the capacity for arousal;
just as faith and the mind, though arising simultaneously, are said to have the capacity to purify the mind,
this case is likewise so.
Regarding the phrase "contact arises dependent upon that," here "that" refers to the threefold conjunction.
As for "contact arises from that," it is named after its cause.
Because contact arises from the conjunction of those three,
that which brings about their conjunction is designated by the name of its effect;
that is to say, it is called "contact" because the triad of factors comes together through the power of contact.
"Explaining 'that' refers to the interpretation of the aforementioned designation;
it explains the name for the triad of conjunctions at the stage of contact.
Regarding the phrase 'because of the threefold conjunction, all have [the capacity] to produce [feeling] accordingly,' etc."

This means that at the time of the conjunction of the three—faculty, object, and consciousness—each possesses the functional capacity of mental factors conducive to the arising of feeling and so forth; therefore, it is said that they all possess it.
In the state of the conjunction of the three, there exists the capacity for the arising [of feeling].
It is called "transformation" (anyathātva) because it is different from the time when [the atoms] were not yet combined.
It is called "discrimination" (vikalpa) because contact arises resembling that [object].
To say "discrimination" means to experience what resembles the object.
Contact gives rise to a semblance of that [object] and possesses the capacity for subsequent production;
it is called "discrimination" because it experiences what appears as a transformation,
just as a son who resembles his father is said to "discriminate" his father.
This does not refer to the conceptualization that acts as the objective condition (*ālambana*).
"That which can give rise to the non-dual desires of union and separation" explains the previous statement regarding its function (*karman*) of giving rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
In this context, "desire" (chanda) is precisely craving (tṛṣṇā).
That is to say, one gives rise to the desire for union when experiencing agreeable objects,
and one gives rise to the desire for separation when experiencing disagreeable objects.
Taking as its object that which is neither [attractive nor repulsive], it gives rise to a desire that is neither of the two;
"desire that is neither of the two" refers precisely to the desire that is neither for union nor for separation.
This means being able to apprehend the true characteristics of the object, such as its causal nature and so forth.
That is to say, the production of wholesome volition with respect to an object is the characteristic of a correct cause;
the production of unwholesome volition is the characteristic of a false cause;
and the production of neutral volition is the characteristic of a cause that is neither.
The meaning intended here is that volition (cetanā),
by taking the three natures as its objects of the three causes,
accordingly directs one's own mind to perform wholesome actions and so forth.
Regarding the name "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmika*) in the Śrāvaka-vehicle treatises:
"ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to the sphere of activity, which is the mind-king (*citta-rāja*),
because it is the sphere of activity for those mental concomitants (*caitta*).
"Great" refers to the mental factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, because they function throughout minds of all three moral natures.
The mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is the ground for these masters, namely feeling, perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and the rest.
It is called "universal ground" (mahābhūmi).
Since feeling and the other [mental factors] are also factors belonging to the universal ground of the mind,
they are termed "universal mental factors" (mahābhūmika-dharma).
This dharma is universal across the three natures and the mind and its concomitants;
it is called a "universal mental factor" (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).
This is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Therefore, the Abhidharmakośakārikā says:
"Regarding all minds,
it is like the mind that suddenly falls [into an object] when it is not one of the four objects."
Just as when one does not desire the four objects that have been habitually practiced and contemplated, there are no such objects;
in the absence of these four objects, there are no distinct objects at all,
and the mind falls into a state of sudden, unreflective occurrence.
That is to say, there are five types of mental states that arise:
first, the sudden;
second, the seeking.
Third is determination;
fourth is defilement and purity;
fifth is outflow.
When consciousness first falls upon an object, it is called "sudden falling.
Although it takes good or evil as its object, it does not yet discern whether it is good or evil.
Subsequently, "seeking" arises, and once it has recognized whether it is good or evil, [the process continues].
Next, resolve arises;
once resolved, defilement and purification arise.
One dwells in malice toward enemies.
One dwells in friendliness toward friends,
in equanimity toward neutral persons,
and after a single moment, a mind of the same nature arises, which is called a "resultant" (niṣyanda) mind.
Among the five types of consciousness,
desire and the other mental factors arise only after a defiled or pure mind; therefore,
at the initial moment of falling into the state of sudden perception (*saṃtīraṇa-citta*), there are no distinct objects.
Regarding the statement, "Although shame and so forth are wholesome, they are not pure because their characteristics are not [pure]," this addresses an external objection.
That is to say, there is an objection that says:
If it is said that the purity of the mind is what is called faith,
then if purity is itself the mind, it should not be a mental factor (*caitta*).
Furthermore, if it is that which purifies the mind, how does it differ from shame (*hrī*) and the other [virtuous mental factors]?
Since shame (*hrī*) and other qualities can also purify the mind,
how is it that faith alone is described as "purity of mind"?
To resolve this difficulty, this passage was written.
Regarding the phrase "by the power of one's own dharma" and so forth:
"self" refers to one's own person;
"dharma" refers to the teaching.
According to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*,
shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) arise based on three types of supremacy (*adhipati*).
The first is supremacy with respect to oneself (*svādhipati*).
These are the persons of superior grade.
Guarding themselves, they refrain from all evil;
thus, two factors predominate.
Among these, the person of middling capacity,
in order to protect the holy teaching, refrains from committing various evils and becomes a sovereign over the three worlds.
This refers to individuals of inferior capacity who,
out of concern for worldly reputation and gain, refrain from committing various evils;
they now give rise to a sense of shame based on their own personal standards.
One gives rise to a sense of shame based on worldly power;
those who revere the virtuous and good—
where "virtuous" refers to the noble sages.
"Good" refers to wholesome dharmas;
"venerating" means honoring the worthy;
"revering" means valuing the good.
Alternatively, both the worthy and the good are held in high esteem.
Those who lack shame and remorse below despise and reject the worthy and the good;
one should understand that those who revere the violent and the wicked are to be treated accordingly.
Regarding "existence and the instruments of existence":
"existence" refers to the fruit of the three realms of existence;
"the instruments of existence" refers to the causes for birth within those realms.
"Suffering" refers to the three types of suffering.
That which gives rise to these three sufferings is called an "instrument of suffering.
As for the statement that the contemplation of existence and so forth is established without necessarily depending on those [instruments], [it means as follows]:
The preceding and following passages also address external objections.
That is to say, there is an objection which states:
"If one is non-attached toward existence, then one would not be free from aversion toward suffering."
If one is without aversion toward suffering, one will likewise not be attached to existence;
therefore, non-attachment and non-hatred cannot arise simultaneously.
How, then, can it be said that these two are both universal to wholesome minds?
Therefore, this distinction is established.
For instance, when shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) honor what is wholesome, they necessarily reject what is unwholesome;
and when they reject what is unwholesome, they necessarily honor what is wholesome.
It is not necessary to separately contemplate the two objects of good and evil to give rise to two distinct minds;
it is the same here as well:
when one is without attachment toward existence, one will necessarily be without aversion toward suffering.
When one is free from aversion toward suffering, one is necessarily free from attachment toward existence.
It is with reference to this that these two names are spoken;
it is not necessary for non-attachment and the other [wholesome roots] to arise through two distinct minds separately observing existence and suffering.
Therefore, non-attachment and non-hatred are said to be co-extensive with all wholesome minds; that is to say,
"the initial generation of the mind" refers to the first arousal of the great vow,
while "cultivation over a long period" refers to practicing for three great eons.
Constant practice without interruption is called uninterrupted cultivation (*nirantara-bhāvanā*).
Cultivating with reverence toward the practice is called earnest cultivation (*satkṛtya-bhāvanā*).
Cultivating without any lapse in practice is called exhaustive cultivation (*aśeṣa-bhāvanā*).
Based on these five types of cultivation, the five kinds of diligence are explained.
Regarding the phrase "distancing oneself from heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and bringing the body and mind into harmony," there are two types of heaviness.
First, the two obstacles;
second, the seeds— these are established under the name of "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*).
First, it is an unfitness of nature due to its opposition to subtlety and lightness.
Second, it is the state of unfitness within the body induced by the seeds of the two obscurations;
this is neither identical to nor different from the five aggregates.
Yet, apart from the five aggregates, there is no separate intrinsic nature [to this].
It causes the body and mind to be dull, heavy, and lacking in tranquility;
because it opposes subtlety and lightness, it is also termed *dauṣṭhulya* (coarseness/heaviness).
In this present passage, that which is to be abandoned is explained as being the latter [state] rather than the former.
The phrase "causing the basis of reliance to become more peaceful and comfortable" is an explanation of the term "transformation of the basis" (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) from the preceding text.
The "transformation of the basis" (āśraya-parāvṛtti) mentioned in the preceding text does not refer to the meaning of the transformation of the basis that constitutes the fruit of Buddhahood,
because it is distinct from those ten types of transformation of the basis.
In this context, the "basis" refers to the body and mind that serve as the support.
As for what is called "transformation," it is named "transformation of the basis" because one transforms away from the state of unease and arrives at a state of well-being.
Regarding the phrase "abiding in equanimity, rectitude, and effortlessness":
"equanimity" refers to the cultivation of relinquishment in the initial stage.
This is because through relinquishment, the mind is freed from the state of imbalance, such as dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*).
Having first realized the equality of the mind,
"uprightness" refers to the state of equanimity (*upekṣā*) as the middle way.
Furthermore, by means of equanimity, the equalized mind is freed from deliberate application (*prayoga*), such that it continues spontaneously.
Subsequently, one realizes the nature of mental equanimity and dwells without effort;
this explains the stage following the relinquishment (*upekṣā*).
Furthermore, by means of this relinquishment, the upright mind becomes free from any apprehension regarding all defilements.
Finally, one realizes the state of dwelling without effort (*anābhoga-vihāra*).

Because it possesses these three meanings, it is distinguished from all other forms of equanimity (*upekṣā*) among the three types of feeling; thus, it is called "equanimity as an application" (*praśrabdya-upekṣā*).
Although it fully subsumes them, it has no separate substantial entity.
"Delight" (*prāmodya*) refers to a portion of non-hatred (*adveṣa*) associated with desire (*chanda*),
because it does not increase hostility toward a desired object.
"Disenchantment" (*nirveda*) refers to a portion of non-attachment (*alobha*) associated with wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because one does not become attached to objects that are to be reviled,
it should be understood that non-avarice, non-hypocrisy, and so forth are likewise [the result].
Non-conceit is subsumed under a portion of moral shame (*hrī*).
If one honors and respects others and does not treat them with pride,
then being free from doubt is subsumed under right wisdom (*samyagprajñā*),
because one who possesses right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is without hesitation.
The absence of resentment and so forth is subsumed under non-hatred (*adveṣa*),
because it directly opposes one aspect of hatred such as anger (*krodha*). Since concealment (*mrakṣa*),
deception (*māyā*), and guile (*śāṭhya*) have one aspect of greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*) as their essential nature, [they are likewise subsumed].
Since non-deception, lack of guile, and so forth are subsumed within portions of non-attachment and non-delusion, they are all fully included therein;
yet, because they possess no separate essence, characteristic, or function, they are not established as distinct [mental factors] despite being conceptually differentiated.
Regarding the ten [mental factors] and the five feelings being all capable of association:
this is the section on association with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayoga-mukha*).
When practicing asceticism, it is because of the presence of faith (*śraddhā*).
Because one feels anxiety regarding falling into the evil destinies in future lives;
because the mind rejoices in the existence of virtuous fruits through faith;
and because there is also faith during times of equanimity.
Since this is the case for faith, the others may be understood by analogy;
all [faculties] consist of the three factors: training and so forth.
Regarding the gate of the classification of the trainings (*śikṣā*) and so forth:
although the treatises of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna fully explain the meaning of these three trainings,
there are differences in their breadth and scope.
For instance, according to the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna,
the conditioned and untainted (anāsrava) factors within the body of a person in training are collectively termed "in-training" (śaikṣa),
while the conditioned and untainted factors within the body of one beyond training are all termed "beyond-training" (aśaikṣa).
All contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) and all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are collectively termed "neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee" (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*) dharmas.
Now, the Mahāyāna school is somewhat broader than that:
all conditioned wholesome dharmas within the person of a trainee (*śaikṣa*) are termed "trainee" (*śaikṣa*).
All conditioned wholesome dharmas within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are called "beyond training.
All remaining wholesome dharmas are called "neither-training-nor-beyond-training" dharmas.
It should be understood that the eleven wholesome dharmas mentioned here are likewise so designated.
Because it is designated according to the bodies of those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and other bodies;
as for "not to be abandoned by vision" (*na darśana-prahātavya*) and so forth,
this is the section on the analysis of the three types of abandonment.
Because these factors, such as faith, are both untainted (*anāsrava*) and tainted (*sāsrava*),
they are subsumed under both what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and what is not to be abandoned (*aheya*).
Even though they are tainted, because they do not involve delusion regarding the principles (*tattva*), they are not abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).
However, because they are delusions regarding phenomena, they are abandoned gradually during the path of cultivation.
As for those that are untainted (*anāsrava*), since they are what is correctly cultivated and not something to be abandoned, they are not subject to abandonment.
The phrase "because the aggregates of grasping arise through the power of craving" explains the meaning of the previous statement that birth is characterized by suffering as its function.
All afflictions (*kleśa*) are termed "grasping" (*upādāna*).
The aggregates arise from grasping, and are therefore called the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*).
These aggregates of grasping are the cause of all suffering;
these very aggregates of grasping previously arose from craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Therefore, it is said that one does not take birth in an undesirable state and so forth.
As for the statement, "By means of ignorance, doubt, false certainty,
and so on," this explains the sense of being the basis for the defilements (*saṃkleśa*).
All afflictions (saṃkleśa) are of three kinds:
first, the affliction of mental defilements (kleśa-saṃkleśa);
second, the affliction of karma (karma-saṃkleśa).
Regarding the defilements of the three births,
what is here referred to as doubt, wrong resolve,
and the afflictions and secondary afflictions such as attachment, and so forth.
This is the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*).
Among these, wrong concentration (*mithyāsamādhi*) consists of the five views (*pañcadṛṣṭi*);
greed and so forth consist of hatred (*dveṣa*) and pride (*māna*).
What is called "action" (karma) refers to the defilement of action.
Action consists of the three types of action:
meritorious action, non-meritorious action, and immovable action.
Meritorious karma refers to the general karma of humans and devas within the desire realm, as well as the specific karma of the five destinies, such as,
for example, the temporary encounter with a cool breeze touching the body while in hell.
Furthermore, as with the various sufferings in hell being termed "wholesome karma" when they are slight,
so too is non-meritorious karma, such as the non-interruption of wholesome roots and the like.
The general and specific karmas that lead to the three evil destinies,
as well as immovable karma— namely,
all those karmas that produce the ripening results (*vipāka*) of the form and formless realms and can bring about future births.
Defilement (*saṃkleśa*) refers to the karmic maturation (*vipāka-phala*) produced by afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma.
Regarding the seven and nine varieties of this pride (*māna*), as for the "seven prides":
[they are as follows:]...
The *Pañcaskandhaka* states:
first, pride (*māna*);
second, excessive pride (*atimāna*).
3. Pride beyond pride (mānātimāna).
4. Inferiority pride (ūnamāna).
5. False pride (mithyāmāna).
Sixth is the conceit of self (asmimāna).
Seventh is the conceit of overestimation (adhimāna).
As for what is called the ninefold conceit (navavidhamāna):
As stated in the twentieth fascicle of the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, the nineteenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, and the one hundred and ninety-ninth fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*,
all maintain that there are nine types of pride (*māna*).
That is to say: "I am superior," "I am equal," or "I am inferior."
There is a self that is superior;
there is a self that is equal;
there is a self that is inferior.
There is no one superior to me;
there is no one equal to me;
there is no one inferior to me.
Regarding the statement that these arise based on the three grades of self and qualities:
four types of pride arise based on the three grades,
while one type arises based on the lower and middle grades.
This refers to pride itself:
conceiving oneself as superior to those who are inferior,
and conceiving oneself as equal to those who are one's equals.
Because the mind is uplifted,
one kind arises therein in its superior degree; that is,
overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Regarding those who are equal, one considers oneself superior;
regarding those who are superior, one considers oneself equal.
This is because the mind is held in high esteem.
Based on the superior grade, two arise:
namely, pride (māna) and excessive pride (atimāna), as well as the pride of inferiority (ūnamāna).
This refers to one who, regarding those superior to oneself, conceives themselves to be superior.
Because the mind is uplifted by conceiving oneself as inferior when compared to those who are far superior,
one gives rise to the first [type of pride] with respect to oneself.
This refers to the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*).
Because one falsely clings to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being a self,
the mind becomes uplifted.
Regarding virtues, two [types of pride] arise:
namely, false pride (*mithyāmāna*) and overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
These consist in conceiving oneself to possess virtues when, in reality, one lacks them.
One causes the mind to become puffed up through wrong reflection;
or, regarding the sublime dharmas that have been realized, one causes the mind to become puffed up by claiming to have attained what has not yet been attained.
This reveals the basis from which the seven types of pride arise.
As for the basis from which the nine types of pride arise,
according to the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*:
The three types of pride are extracted from among the seven previously mentioned.
Specifically, regarding the former— pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*),
and inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*)— the statement "I am superior" constitutes excessive pride.
To say "I am [equal]" refers to pride (*māna*).
To say "I am inferior" is the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*).
To think "there is one who is superior to me" is also the pride of inferiority.
The thought "I am equal" is called pride (*māna*).
The thought "I am inferior" is called excessive pride (*atimāna*).
The thought "there is no one superior to me" is called pride.
The thought "I am equal to those who are superior" is overweening pride (*atimāna*).
The thought "I am not inferior to those who are superior" is the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*).
Its function is to serve as the basis for all dogmatic views.
Regarding all views:
among the sixty-two views, twenty propositions are categorized according to the past.
They maintain concerning the past as follows:
First, going as it truly is;
second, not going as it truly is;
third, both going as it truly is and not going as it truly is.
Fourth: neither going nor not going.
Regarding the twenty propositions concerning the future:
first, the future has an end.
2. Infinite; 3. Both finite and infinite;
4. Neither finite nor infinite.
Regarding the present twenty propositions:
first, the present is eternal;
second, it is impermanent.
Third, both eternal and impermanent;
fourth, neither eternal nor impermanent.
These are rooted in the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
Each of the three periods has twenty views;
together with the fundamental [view], they constitute the sixty-two views.
"Trend" (gati) refers to the underlying intention.
The sixty-two views all possess an underlying intention;
collectively they are termed "tendencies toward views.
All of them take the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their basis.
Therefore, it is said that its function is to serve as the basis for the various types of views (*dṛṣṭigata*).

Regarding the statement that "these distinctions of views number sixty-five," all of these are established as twenty propositions based upon the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), through the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self (*ātman-ātmīya*).
Regarding the twenty phrases beginning with "sixty-five":
first, based on the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), there are four propositions.
The first is: "Form is the self."
Second, "I have various forms";
third, "forms belong to me";
fourth, "I am within forms."
The first phrase refers to "I";
the remainder refers to "what belongs to me.
This is the case for the aggregate of form; it is likewise for the others.
The same applies to the remaining aggregates.
Since there are four [categories] for each of the five aggregates, this constitutes twenty phrases.
As for the sixty-five:
Taking form as the head, one grasps form as "I" and takes the remaining four aggregates as "mine.
There are thirteen such propositions.
That is to say: "Form is the self" implies the sense of being possessed;
"feeling is my servant" implies the sense of prior subordination;
"feeling is my dwelling" implies the sense of residing therein.
The aggregates of perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all likewise.
Upon each of these four aggregates there are three phrases;
four times three makes twelve.
This constitutes thirteen propositions: "form is my self" and "that which is mine is form.
Next, regarding "feeling is my self," one applies this to the remaining four aggregates as "that which is mine," which likewise constitutes thirteen propositions.
The five aggregates together constitute sixty-five propositions;
these are the aforementioned sixty heterodox views.
This fourth [view] is the school that maintains the self truly exists.
Regarding those who hold the four views of eternalism concerning the past,
these are found in the "Brahmajāla Sūtra" (Fan dong pin) of the *Dīrgha Āgama* and in the eighty-seventh fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Although all [scriptures] explain this in full, there are slight differences;
now, following the *Yogācārabhūmi*, this meaning is clarified as follows:
the recollection of past lives attained through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is categorized as superior, middling, or inferior.
Regarding the views on the past that calculate it as eternal based on distance, there are four theories:
first, recollecting twenty eons of formation and destruction;
second, recollecting forty eons of formation and destruction.
Third, I recall eighty eons of cosmic formation and destruction;
during that time, sentient beings neither increased nor decreased.
For this reason, I know that both myself and the world are entirely eternal.
Fourth, with the divine eye, they see that all sentient beings proceed from the previous world to the subsequent world without interruption; therefore,
they reckon that both the self and the world are entirely eternal.
This refers to the aforementioned thesis that all phenomena are eternal.
Regarding the fourth, the proponents of the "partial eternity" theory:
first, there are those who, having passed away from the Brahma Heaven, come to be born in this world.
By virtue of practicing meditative concentration, one attains the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
When observing their previous abodes, the Brahmā King is still present; yet, not seeing a beginning or an end, he claims to be eternally abiding.
That I have been born here is itself impermanent;
thus one knows that one portion of the world is eternal.
Second, it is heard that the Brahmā King held such a view.
The four great elements are eternal,
while the mind is impermanent.
This [view] was either accepted by him or heard from others through successive transmission.
I take the Brahmā King as my authoritative standard and believe his words;
therefore, I know that one portion of the world is eternal.
Third, there are those who pass away from the Heaven of Laughter (Hasita) and come to be born here.
I have attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives.
Because I did not joke or laugh with those devas, I remained there permanently;
it was because I did joke and laugh that I was born here.
Therefore, one knows that one portion of the world is eternally abiding.

Fourth, there are those who, having passed away from the Heaven of Wrath (Krodhadeva), come to be born in this world and attain the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna).
"Those gods whom we hold to be free from extreme anger dwell there eternally,
whereas we, due to our anger, have been born here;
therefore, one part of the world must be eternal."
This is also the thesis that all phenomena are without cause.
As for the calculation of sixteen [views] regarding the existence of perception in the future limit and so forth,
this is based on what is taught in the Brahmajāla Sūtra.
Furthermore, regarding the first group of sixteen theorists who possess perception:
there are four permutations based on the contrast between the finite and the infinite,
and four permutations based on the contrast with form.
Regarding suffering and pleasure, there are four permutations;
regarding the extent of perception, there are four permutations.
These four sets of four together constitute sixteen propositions.
Regarding the four propositions concerning the first pair of form:
first, that after my death there will be both form and perception;
second, that there will be no form but there will be perception.
Third, those that are both with form and without form, yet possess perception;
fourth, those that are neither with form nor without form, yet possess perception.
Regarding the second pair of extremes, there are four propositions.
1. After my death, I shall exist with a finite consciousness;
2. I shall exist with an infinite consciousness;
3. I shall exist with both finite and infinite consciousness.
Regarding the fourth [category], which is neither finite nor infinite and possesses perception:
as for the four propositions concerning suffering in the third pair, the first is:
"After my death, there is suffering and perception."
Second, there is pleasure and perception;
third, there is both pain and pleasure and perception;
fourth, there is neither pain nor pleasure and perception.
Regarding the four propositions concerning the fourth pair of perceptions:
first, the perception that "after my death, I shall exist as one";
second, the perception of suffering.
Third, because the objects of perception are narrow, there is the notion of "limited perception.
Fourth, because the objects of perception are broad, there is the notion of "immeasurable perception.
These constitute the sixteen theories concerning the existence of perception (*saṃjñā-vāda*). As for the eight [theories] concerning non-perception (*asaṃjñā*):
Regarding form, there are four [alternatives].
Regarding the finite and the infinite, there are likewise four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
As for the four regarding form:
First, that after my death there will be form and no perception;
second, that there will be no form and no perception;
third, that there will be both form and no form and no perception.
Regarding the four alternatives concerning that which is neither material nor immaterial and is non-percipient:
in the second pair of extremes, there are four propositions.
The first is: "After my death, there is an extreme state of non-perception."
Second, the perceptionless [beings] who are infinite;
third, the perceptionless [beings] who are both finite and infinite;
fourth, the perceptionless [beings] who are neither finite nor infinite.
Since there is no perception, it cannot be described as being either suffering or pleasure, or one or many;
therefore, there are only eight propositions. Regarding the eight proponents who maintain that both [suffering and pleasure] do not exist, there are four positions concerning form (*rūpa*).
Regarding the finite and the infinite, there are likewise four propositions.
Regarding form, there are four:
first, that after my death I shall possess form, being neither percipient nor non-percipient.
Second, the self is formless, being neither percipient nor non-percipient;
third, it is both with form and without form, being neither percipient nor non-percipient;
fourth, it is neither with form nor without form, being neither percipient nor non-percipient.
Regarding the four propositions concerning the finite and the infinite in the second pair:
first, "I shall have a finite existence after this life, yet neither-perception-nor-non-perception";
second, "I shall have an infinite existence, yet neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
3. The self is both finite and infinite, and is neither percipient nor non-percipient.
4. The self is neither finite nor infinite, and is neither percipient nor non-percipient.
Since it is neither with perception nor without perception,
one cannot say that there is suffering, pleasure, a single perception, or manifold perceptions; therefore,
there are only eight phrases.
All of these belong to the schools that maintain the self exists as a substantial reality.
Regarding the "seven types of annihilationists" and so forth:
while one has not yet died, there exists a coarse material body.
While that which is composed of the four great elements remains intact and undestroyed,
there is sickness, there are boils, and there are arrows.
Yet, once I have died, it will be annihilated without remainder.
At that time, I have thoroughly severed and extinguished such celestial beings of the realm of desire and celestial beings of the realm of form.
The formless sphere of infinite space, the formless sphere of infinite consciousness,
the sphere of nothingness,
and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
All are utterly annihilated.
Therefore, these are called the seven theories of annihilationism;
they constitute the school of thought asserting that there is annihilation after death.
This refers to those who deny the reality of causes, effects, functions, and substantial entities.
Regarding the denial of causes, it means saying:
"There is no giving, no offering of sustenance, no sacrificial rites, no evil conduct, and no sublime conduct."
To speak of "denying the fruit" means to deny the maturation fruits (*vipākaphala*) and so forth produced by unwholesome conduct and sublime conduct.
To speak of "denying activity" means:
"There is no this world, there is no other world, there is no father, and there is no mother;
these are those who destroy real entities.
This means that there are no true arhats in the world."
This is precisely the school that maintains that both cause and effect are empty.
There are those who cling to the two types of "causeless theories" regarding the past,
asserting that based on the fixed nature of the world and improper reflection, they perceive a lack of continuity as the cause for the infinite variety of internal and external phenomena.
Thus he forms this thought:
"I and the world arise without cause.
This is precisely the prior thesis that all phenomena are without cause.
Regarding the four types of evasive equivocation concerning finitude and so forth:
"the four [views on] finitude" refers to the ninth position mentioned above, the doctrine of finitude and infinity;
"evasive equivocation regarding immortality" refers to the four doctrines of evasive equivocation concerning immortality.
As for those who reckon [the self] as Maheśvara, Lokapāla, Śakra, or Brahmā: Maheśvara is Mahādeva;
Lokapāla refers to the Four Great Heavenly Kings.
"Śakra" refers to Śakra;
"Brahmā" refers to the King Brahmā;
as for the other categories of beings:
The infinitesimal atom (*paramāṇu*), time, space, the primal limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), and the natural void (*ākāśa*) and their like—
these are eternal, permanent, and subject to no change.
That all such phenomena are eternally constant constitutes the fundamental tenet of this school.
Alternatively, those who reckon that Īśvara and others are the cause of all things maintain that the Lord God (Īśvaradeva) is able to produce all phenomena;
the term "and others" includes [such beings as] Mahābrahmā and so forth.
It is also the cause of all things in the world;
this is the thesis that [the world] was created by Īśvara.
Furthermore, there are those who falsely cling to various erroneous conceptions of liberation.
Those who cling to the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the locus of liberation;
or those who falsely cling to what is not the path as being the path;
and those other than those with [wrong] views who falsely cling to various phenomena as the true path.
All of these are false conceptualizations regarding the doctrine of purity.
That is to say, concerning various views and the aggregates upon which they depend,
one clings to the view that has arisen as being supreme and capable of attaining purity.
Since views are thus,
they arise based on the body;
this body, which is the basis for these views, consists of the five aggregates.
This is also the most supreme means for attaining purification.
Having grasped one's own self as supreme and capable of purification,
one then views others as inferior and not capable of purification.
From this, various forms of strife and contention arise;
therefore, this adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is itself a dharma of strife.
That is to say, it concerns those precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) that accord with various [wrong] views.
Since they previously clung to views as being supreme and capable of purification,
they adopted various precepts and observances in accordance with those views;
they then likewise clung to these precepts and the body composed of the five aggregates upon which the precepts depend as being supreme and pure.
"Grasping at precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) refers to "grasping," which means attachment.
Regarding the phrase "born in a lower realm and not yet free from the defilements of that lower realm," the afflictions of the lower and higher realms differ vastly in their coarseness and subtlety.
When the afflictions of the lower [levels] have not been severed, the afflictions of the upper [levels] do not arise;
rather, it is necessary for the afflictions of the lower levels to be suppressed for the afflictions of the upper levels to manifest.
Having stated this in general, to explain it in detail:
Just as the first dhyāna is called a lower stage,
when one cultivates the second dhyāna but has not yet attained its fundamental state and regresses to be reborn in one's own [original] stage,
it is therefore said that one is "born in a lower stage."
If one has not yet abandoned the afflictions of the first dhyāna,
the afflictions of the second dhyāna will not arise; however,
if one attains the fundamental concentration (mauladhyāna) of the second stage, [they will cease].
One subdues the afflictions of the lower stages of the first dhyāna;
however, the defilements of the higher stages manifest within the second dhyāna.
As it is with the lower and higher [stages] in these two dhyānas, so it is likewise for the others.

It should be understood that the same applies when one suppresses the lower levels and arises in the higher ones, such as the third and fourth dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
Regarding those born in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the fourth dhyāna who disparage liberation and so forth:
This clarifies that afflictions which give rise to karma are produced by the conceptualization of one born in a higher realm looking down upon a lower one.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"In the past, there was a bhikṣu of little learning."
Without studying the sūtras or śāstras, they directly cultivate meditative concentration and attain the first dhyāna, claiming to have attained the first fruit;
continuing in this manner until they realize the fourth dhyāna, they claim, "I have attained the fruit of arhatship."
Having already attained that meditative concentration and being destined to be born in that heaven,
and having subsequently reached the end of his life and being about to be reborn there,
he then gives rise to slanderous speech within his intermediate state body (antarābhava).
"An Arhat has already exhausted the conditions for further birth;
how then can I now have birth?
Therefore, one knows that there is no true liberation in the world."
However, these are the false claims of the wise;
by slandering liberation, one immediately transforms into an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) of hell and falls into hell.
Since that intermediate state belongs to the fourth dhyāna, [it is not subject to the fires of hell].
The slander and disparagement that arise are the afflictions that project karma belonging to a lower stage;
therefore, one born in a higher stage can give rise to the discriminative afflictions of a lower stage.
Regarding the phrase "when one is in a higher stage and is about to be born [into a lower one]," etc.:
This demonstrates that the innate afflictions arising from the higher realms to moisten birth in the lower realms function as follows:
when one is about to descend from a higher realm to be born below,
one must first give rise to craving to moisten the karma of the lower realm before being reborn there.
Because the Sūtra states that one is not born through non-desire or non-acceptance,
and since one moistens lower karma by giving rise to desire for the lower realms,
we know that in the higher stages, one gives rise to innate afflictions that moisten birth in those higher realms.

Regarding the statement, "those who grasp at self and what belongs to the self with respect to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) through views of permanence and annihilation, pride, and so forth":
this indicates that the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and pride (*māna*) can take higher objects as their referents.
These three afflictions, however, when considered as innate (*sahaja*), cannot function by taking distinct individual objects.
Taking the upper realms as its general object, the grasping at "I" and "mine" abandons the notion of impermanence and clings to permanence;
it then gives rise to pride by upholding the phenomena of those levels.
As for the remaining five [defilements] taking the upper realms as their objects, this principle is thoroughly established.
Regarding the "remaining five," they are:
first, delusion;
second, doubt.
3. False view; 4.
Adherence to views; 5.
Adherence to precepts and observances.
Furthermore, these five types of teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna all allow for the taking of those above as objects;
because this is commonly accepted, it is said to be "established by consensus" (*prasiddha*).
Regarding those born in the higher realms who, relying on their own superior virtues, look down upon sentient beings below: [the text addresses this].
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 59, states:
"Those born in the higher realms, with respect to the sentient beings of the lower realms,
possess the merit of being constantly and joyfully secluded."
"To consider oneself superior and to hold others in contempt" refers to the pride of self-exaltation.

Regarding the phrase "those who, based on the totality of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), grasp at a self and what belongs to a self, and [cling to] annihilationism, eternalism, craving, and so forth":

this demonstrates that the innate view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) belonging to the higher realms, as well as craving, also take lower realms as their objects.
This means that innate views (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*) cannot discern individual objects;
therefore, they take the lower realms as their object in their entirety,
conceiving all phenomena as "self" and "mine," and giving rise to craving through the grasping at annihilation or permanence.

Regarding the statement that "doubt and the latter three views should be considered according to reason," this means that one wonders whether the lower suffering and so forth exist or do not exist; thus,
it is known that when doubt arises, one immediately negates [the existence of] them as being non-existent.
This is subsumed under wrong view.
Because one clings to all views and precepts of that desire realm as being supreme and as causes, there are two types of grasping.
However, the true path of vision (darśanamārga) takes the truths collectively as its object.
The path of seeing is twofold.
First is the true path of seeing,
which refers to the fundamental non-conceptual wisdom itself.
Arising immediately after the preceding preparatory application,
it directly realizes the two kinds of emptiness and directly severs the two kinds of hindrances;
because it first illuminates the principle, it is called the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Second is the path of insight characterized by images (*sākāra-darśanamārga*),
which is the subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) arising immediately after the path of insight characterized by reality (*tattva-darśanamārga*).
The true path of seeing consists of the uninterrupted and liberated paths;
because it cuts off delusions and realizes the principle, it is also called the path of seeing.
This true path of seeing is without signs (*animitta*).
Taking the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all four truths as its collective object,
a single path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) universally severs the afflictions of conceptual discrimination regarding the four truths,
abandoning them all at once and simultaneously.

Regarding the phrase "because suffering and its origin are the causal basis for those," it means that these ten types [of views] all arise as false views through delusion regarding suffering and its origin; therefore,
they constitute the causal conditions and the basis upon which those [views] depend.
Due to the power of the afflictions, one takes pleasure in and clings to saṃsāra;
because one perceives the realm of nirvāṇa as a precipice and gives rise to great fear,
the two views of self-identity and extremes arise only with respect to the fruit.
This explanation shows that these two views are exclusively deluded regarding the meaning of suffering.
That is to say, there are two causes for these two [views] being deluded about suffering:

first, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) operates through coarse and shallow perceptions and is not strong or investigative; therefore, it arises only with respect to the fruit [of suffering].
Second, the distinction between emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and selflessness (*anātman*): they belong to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
That is to say, emptiness and selflessness have both general and specific applications;
generally, all four truths are empty.
It is called "empty" because it is neither self nor belongs to a self.
It is called "non-self" because all things are devoid of a self.
Specifically, the five aggregates of the truth of suffering, being associated with outflows, lack the nature of a self; therefore, they are termed "non-self."

It is because they are not "mine" that they are said to be empty. The view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is a specific delusion regarding the five contaminated aggregates; because they are empty and not a self, one clings to them as "I" and "mine.
The view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) is a specific delusion regarding the five contaminated aggregates; by clinging to permanence or annihilation, it contradicts the nature of arising and ceasing.
Therefore, these two views are deluded only regarding the Truth of Suffering.
That is to say, among the three views, doubt and the [other] views directly delude one regarding the principle of suffering;
specifically, they doubt whether the Truth of Suffering exists or does not exist.
The view of a self-body clings to a self and is thus deluded regarding the principle of non-self;
the view of extremes clings to annihilationism or eternalism and is thus deluded regarding the principle of arising and ceasing;
wrong view denies that all things in the present and future are suffering.
Therefore, these four types of immediate delusion regarding the principle of suffering consist of the two grasps (*parāmarśa*),
which cling to those three views, asceticism and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and their underlying aggregates as being supreme and capable of purification.
This explains the meaning of the two grasps as remote delusions regarding suffering.
That is to say, the grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) clings to the three preceding views;
the grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) clings to those various views,
as well as to the precepts, observances, and the aggregates upon which they depend, regarding them as supreme and capable of purification.
Because these three views arise from being separated by, related to, and deluded regarding [the object] respectively,
they are thus remote delusions rather than direct delusions.
Regarding the arising of attachment and so forth toward one's own views, those of others, and their respective associates, it should be understood accordingly in that order.
In this context, what is revealed is that greed, hatred, and pride are the three non-friendlies that are deluded regarding the truths;
"one's own views" refers to the aforementioned three views arising within one's own continuum;
and "retinue" refers to the mind and mental factors that arise simultaneously with those views.
Regarding "seeing that [view]": this refers to the three aforementioned views arising from one's own person.
Their associated factors (*parivāra*) are the same as before;
that is, one gives rise to craving and attachment toward one's own view and its associated factors.
If one gives rise to anger toward the retinue seen in others,
and gives rise to pride toward the retinue seen in oneself and others,
it is therefore said that they arise respectively and accordingly.
Regarding the statement that "associated ignorance is deluded in the same way as the nine [types of delusion], while uncommon ignorance is directly deluded":
the term "ignorance" (ajñāna) is itself nescience (avidyā).
However, this nescience is generally of two kinds.
First, the associated [afflictions],
which are universally concomitant with the various afflictions of the six consciousnesses;
second, the non-associated [afflictions].
It does not coexist with the various consciousnesses or the various afflictions;
furthermore, this "unshared" [nature] is of two kinds:
first, that which is constantly active (*nitya-pravṛtti*).
The first exists only in the manas;
the second, "acting alone," exists only in the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
Furthermore, this solitary [ignorance] is of two kinds.
The first is that which is primary,
being solitary and deluded regarding the principles of reality, rather than arising in conjunction with craving and the other afflictions.
Second, it is not primary.
Regarding the statement that it is not associated with greed and so forth, but is associated with anger and so forth:
herein, since the association [of the mind] follows all the various afflictions, [it is not restricted].

Regarding the various afflictions, there is a distinction between those that are proximate and those that are remote in their delusion regarding the Truths. If an affliction is associated with a proximate delusion, it is a proximate delusion regarding the Truths;
if it is associated with a remote delusion, it is a remote delusion regarding the Truths.
The non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) mentioned here is that which serves as the primary factor among the "solitary" (*kevala*) types;
it is to be abandoned solely by the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*).
Their ignorance regarding the principles of the Truths is not primary,
as it functions independently and is abandoned through both cultivation and insight; thus,
for a certain class of Śrāvakas, [the afflictions] of each of the nine grades across the nine stages of the three realms are eliminated gradually and sequentially.
That is to say, the three realms are divided into nine stages:
the desire realm, the four dhyānas, and the four formless attainments.
Within each stage, there are nine grades of afflictions.
The nine times nine together constitute eighty-one categories.
For those of dull faculties, these arise separately as eighty-one categories.
Through each successive stage of the Noble Path, one gradually eliminates these eighty-one categories of afflictions.
By abandoning six grades of desire, one attains the fruit of a once-returner;
by abandoning nine grades of desire, one attains the fruit of a non-returner;
and by abandoning all [defilements] of the higher realms, one attains the fruit of arhatship.
Within each stage (bhūmi),
the first eight categories [of afflictions] are all abandoned by means of both the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*),
because there is a distinction between those that are deluded regarding principles (*li*) and those that are deluded regarding phenomena (*shi*).
If the ninth grade of the fundamental wisdom is severed,
it is because it is subtle and difficult to sever due to its exclusive delusion regarding principle (*tattva*).
For those of sharp faculties, the eighty-one grades across the nine stages are combined into nine clusters.
The ninefold noble path brings about the distinct abandonment of the nine grades [of afflictions].
That is to say, the superior-grade afflictions of the nine stages are combined into a single aggregate and abandoned by a single noble path.

In this manner, up to the point where the lowest-of-the-low grade of afflictions within the ninth stage is consolidated into a single mass and suddenly severed by the arising of the highest-of-the-high grade of the noble path;
having severed six grades of the desire realm, one becomes a Once-returner.
Because the six grades of the upper eight stages are all abandoned,
one transcends the fruit of Once-returner without entering it;
by abandoning the nine grades of the desire realm, one becomes a Non-returner.
Because the nine grades of the upper eight stages are all abandoned,
one transcends the fruit of non-returner without attaining it;
one transcends the two intermediate fruits and achieves the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
Although there are differences between the sharp and dull faculties regarding their transcendence of the gradual stages,
at the time of severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), both arise simultaneously as the two paths of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*);
for it is the mind that distinguishes the severance of afflictions and the realization of principle.
Regarding the phrase "that causes easy understanding and this causes easy focalization":
"understanding" refers to practical comprehension (*pratipatti*). It means that practical comprehension undergoes transformation.
"Condition" refers to the object of cognition (*ālambana*).
When the object of cognition changes,
a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) is applied therein.
First, easy understanding but difficult conditions:
first calculating that form is permanent, and subsequently calculating that form is annihilated.
Second, easy conditions but difficult understanding.
First one conceives of form as permanent, and subsequently conceives of sensation as permanent;
these three modes of understanding the object are all easy.
First one conceives of form as permanent, and subsequently conceives of sensation as subject to cessation.
The four modes of understanding their objects are all unchanging;
they reckon the preceding and succeeding moments of form as permanent and so forth.
As for the statement that these are not afflictions but are merely defiled and coarse: [it means they are not fundamental afflictions].
This section on exclusion and establishment clarifies that, for three reasons, only twenty [mental factors] are taught.
First, by specifying that they are not root afflictions, greed and the other six afflictions are excluded.
Second, by specifying that they are exclusively defiled, the universal [factors] are excluded.
Because the object-specific (*viṣayaviniyata*) and indeterminate (*aniyata*) [mental factors] pertain to all three moral natures (*tridhātu*),
the latter [the secondary afflictions] are distinguished as merely coarse and manifest, excluding those such as outbursts of anger (*pradāśa*);
furthermore, they are established based on the specific states (*avasthā*) of anger and the other [secondary afflictions].
Regarding the middle two [categories], all unwholesome minds may, as appropriate, give rise to both small and great [defilements] together.
This refers to what is explained below:
the seven small [defilements] are comprised exclusively within the category of the unwholesome nature.
The three minor and eight major [mental factors] are common to both natures.
Since the seven minor [factors] are subsumed under the nature of unwholesomeness,
they arise in association with both of the middle two [natures].
Regarding the three minor, three major, and eight unwholesome [mental factors],
which are unwholesome by nature, and the two intermediate [factors] associated with the indeterminate (avyākṛta) nature:
the phrase "as the case may be" (*yathāyogam*) is placed to clarify that these do not arise simultaneously with the two intermediate [factors].
Since it is granted that the eight great [mental factors] pervade all defiled minds and may arise successively within each of the minor ones,
this means that while "defiled" (kliṣṭa) is broad, "unwholesome" (akuśala) is narrow;
for "defiled" encompasses both the unwholesome and the neutral (avyākṛta) natures.
Therefore, while all that is unwholesome (*akuśala*) is necessarily a defiled mind (*kliṣṭacitta*),
there are defiled minds that are not unwholesome.
For this reason, the eight universal [mental factors] pervade all defiled minds.
Since they are both associated with the two natures of the indeterminate and the unwholesome,
they are present in both the small and medium [degrees] due to their unwholesome nature;
this is because those ten [factors] of the small degree do not arise simultaneously.
Thus, these eight [mental factors] are mutually associated.
Regarding those that are associated with the five feelings among the intermediate [mental factors]:
this means that the five feelings can coexist with all three moral natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate).
The eight great secondary afflictions associated with the defiled-neutral state arise together with the eight [mental factors].
Within the category of the unwholesome nature, both [the primary and secondary afflictions] arise together.
Since the eight great secondary afflictions pervade all three realms and all six consciousnesses, they are associated with all five feelings.
Although the middle two [categories] are comprised solely within the desire realm,
they are associated with the five feelings because they coexist with the six consciousnesses;
as for the five dharmas such as anger (*krodha*), they coexist with four [feelings], excluding pleasure (*sukha*).
The five are anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāśa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*).
They exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and do not extend to the four dhyānas, as there is no pleasure of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) there.
They are not concomitant with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), nor are they accompanied by bodily pleasure (*kāyika-sukha*).
In the miserable realms (durgati), anger and other such states arising from mental suffering coexist with all five feelings;
therefore, it is said that anger and the others are associated with four feelings, excluding pleasure (*sukha*).
As for the five dharmas beginning with guile (*śāṭhya*), they may be associated with all five feelings.
The five are flattery (*śāṭhya*), deception (*māyā*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), arrogance (*mada*), and stinginess (*mātsarya*).
Although they do not correspond with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*),
there exists a mental-sphere pleasure (*manobhūmi-sukha*) that extends throughout the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*).
Furthermore, since it also extends to the miserable realms and the mental states of suffering,
it is said that flattery (*śāṭhya*) and the like may be associated with all five feelings.
As for the distinction between pride (*māna*) and conceit (*mada*), the latter is associated exclusively with delusion (*moha*).
That is to say, because delusion (*moha*) is universally associated with all afflictions, it coexists with pride (*māna*).
*Mada* (intoxication) takes its own nature as its object and consists of stained attachment and haughty arrogance;
*māna* takes the stages [of existence] as its object and arises as an elevation of self that looks down upon others.
Since their modes of activity and resolutions are distinct, they cannot arise simultaneously.
Among the seven minor [unwholesome roots], two are exclusively unwholesome:
namely, anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāśa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*).
Because the mental aspects (*ākāra*) of the desire realm alone are coarse,
the meaning of the two intermediate unwholesome [factors] can be understood.
As for the three minor and eight great [factors], they also pertain to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Because flattery (*śāṭhya*), deceit (*māyā*), and pride (*mada*) pervade all three realms;
and because the eight great defilements of falling (*pātayantikā-kleśa*) universally taint the mind,
they are not only unwholesome (*akuśala*) but also extend to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding the statement that "flattery and deception exist in the desire realm and the form realm, while the others pervade all three realms":
what is referred to as the "form realm" here is the first dhyāna.
This [realm] and the lower realms possess flattery and deception because kings and ministers arise therein.
Pride and the eight great [universal] factors pervade all three realms because their modes of activity are universal;
they are not like contact and the others, which are necessarily universal to the mind.
He then provided a difficult and weighty re-explanation:
regarding what was previously stated— that [the nature of] the wholesome, the defiled, and so forth, are all indeterminate—
the term "and so forth" (等) includes both the mind (*citta*) and the stage (*bhūmi*).
These four are not only indeterminate with respect to the three natures;
they are also indeterminate across various minds and stages.
Therefore, it is said that they are not like contact and so forth, which are determinately pervasive and so on.
Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharmakośa* that greed, anger, pride, and doubt are added [to the universal mental factors] according to the specific levels (*bhūmi*) where they occur:
as for "the level being indeterminate," this means that these do not,
like the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), each individually pervade all states of mind.
